I've been farming this land for 30 years. I know Quzhou's soil — it's mostly sandy loam, the summers are hot and dry, and if you don't irrigate right, you lose the crop. My well gives me control that rain-dependent farmers don't have. That matters.

My main cash crop is cotton. I've grown cotton most of my life. It's labor-intensive but it pays better than grain. With my son working in the city now and it being just me and my husband, I can't overextend myself. So I keep cotton at 5.5 mu and put the remaining 4 mu in wheat-maize rotation — wheat over winter, then maize after I harvest the wheat in June. That way the grain land works twice a year.

For cotton, I'll plough deep this spring — I always do, it breaks up the hardpan and cotton roots need depth. I'll use hybrid Bt seed, same type I've used for years. It handles bollworm better and I don't have to spray as many times. Five pesticide sprays across the season — aphids early, bollworm mid-season, spider mites in the heat. I'll irrigate four times: before planting to wet the seedbed, then at bud stage, flowering, and boll development. Potassium is important for fiber quality so I put more K on cotton than grain.

For wheat, I rotary-till the soil in October after cotton is cleared from those 4 mu. I use an improved local variety — reliable, disease-tolerant. Three irrigations: a winter freeze-protection watering in November, then jointing and heading. Two pesticide applications, mostly for rust and aphids in spring.

Maize goes in right after wheat harvest in June — no-till, straight into the stubble. My husband handles most of the maize since it's low maintenance. Hybrid seed. Two irrigations only — the summer rains help, and maize in Hebei doesn't need as much as cotton. Two pesticide sprays for corn borer.

I keep inputs moderate. Fertilizer prices have gone up and my household income from off-farm work helps, but I don't want to overspend on inputs and squeeze the margin.
